description: A teenager finding herself between an absent mother, a kind queer friend and a brief sailor lover.
content_html:
A Cast of Arrivals and Departures

Every character in A Taste of Honey either arrives and leaves, or is left behind. Shelagh Delaney’s five-character study maps a world in which no relationship is secure and every connection is temporary. As a performer or director, understanding each character’s function in this structure of departure is essential to every staging decision. The way characters move through space — proxemics — tells the audience about power and need before a single line is spoken.

Jo

Jo is seventeen, sharp-tongued and quietly terrified. She has literary ambitions — she notices the wallpaper, she reads, she wants to become an art student — but she is surrounded by a world that does not accommodate that ambition. As a performer playing Jo, you are balancing two registers simultaneously: a caustic wit that Jo deploys as self-protection, and an underlying fear and longing she rarely allows the audience to see directly. In the early scenes with Helen, Jo keeps physical distance — rarely upstage of her mother, often crossing to the window or the door as if planning an exit. In the scenes with the Boy, the performer might gradually reduce that distance: a tentative step closer, a hand movement that almost reaches out, the body language of someone discovering trust for the first time.

Vocally, Jo uses pace and pitch as armour. A performer might deliver her sharpest lines at speed, running the words together to prevent silence — and then allow a sudden stillness, a lowered volume, when something genuine escapes. Contrast between those two registers, anchored to specific moments, is what makes Jo's character legible across the play’s emotional range. A costume designer might keep Jo in the same school coat throughout Act One — slightly too small, buttons straining — as a visual signal that childhood is ending whether Jo is ready or not.

Key Fact

Jo operates on two registers: defensive wit (fast pace, raised pitch, movement away from other characters) and suppressed vulnerability (stillness, lowered volume, reduced proxemic distance). A skilled performer must make the audience feel both even when Jo herself is suppressing one of them.

Helen

Helen is Jo’s mother — semi-alcoholic, restless, charismatic, and largely absent in every sense that matters. She has made her own choices for survival in post-war Salford and those choices have not included being the mother Jo needed. Delaney asks us not to condemn Helen but to understand her: she is a woman shaped by limited options, not a villain. A performer playing Helen must resist the temptation to make her cruel. She loves Jo in the way she is capable of loving — intermittently, distractedly, warmly when she remembers to be. Physically, Helen takes up space: she moves with an ease and confidence that Jo does not have, occupying downstage centre as if it belongs to her.

When Helen returns in Act Two, a director might use her positioning relative to Geof to communicate the power shift that her arrival represents. Helen and Geof never really share the stage comfortably — a director might use tableau moments when the three of them are present to make the tension in that triangle spatial and visible. Helen’s costume might contrast with Jo’s: brighter colour, more embellishment, a deliberate performance of femininity that echoes and ironises Jo’s situation.

Peter is Helen’s boyfriend and then husband: older, wealthier, given to cruelty. His function in the play is partly structural — he takes Helen away from Jo — and partly thematic: he embodies the economic and sexual power that men of his class and age exercised over women like Helen. A performer playing Peter might use physical bulk and slow, deliberate movement to communicate his dominance, occupying space in the flat as if he already owns it before Helen has agreed to his proposal.

Peter is not on stage for large portions of the play, which means his appearances should feel imposing and slightly alien in a world that is primarily Jo and Helen’s. A lighting designer might use a cooler, harder lighting special during Peter’s scenes to contrast with the warmer domestic light of the flat’s other moments — a subtle signal to the audience that his presence changes the atmosphere.

Geof

Geof is a young queer art student who befriends Jo and moves in to look after her during her pregnancy. He is the play’s moral centre: caring, patient, domestic in the best sense. In 1958 Britain, homosexuality was a criminal offence — a fact that makes Geof’s vulnerability and courage explicit for the audience. He risks a great deal by the simple act of building a life in that flat with Jo. A performer playing Geof might communicate this through a physical watchfulness — a slight self-containment in public scenes, a contrasting ease and openness in the private scenes between him and Jo. The tenderness of the scenes when Jo and Geof make a home together is the play’s warmest section, and a director should stage this warmth carefully: close proxemics, gentle overlapping movement, the actors working in parallel rather than against each other.

Key Fact

Geof is queer at a time when homosexuality was illegal in Britain (it would not be partially decriminalised until 1967). His choice to move in with Jo and care for her is an act of courage and solidarity that the 1958 audience would have understood as dangerous. Examiners reward students who contextualise Geof beyond a simple “kind friend” reading.

The Boy — sometimes called Jimmie — is a Black sailor on shore leave who has a brief winter affair with Jo. He is one of the earliest sympathetic Black characters in mainstream British theatre, presented without exoticism or stereotype. His relationship with Jo is genuine and tender; the fact that he leaves is structural, not a moral failing. Delaney’s decision to name him simply “the Boy” in the script’s first appearance is sometimes discussed by directors as a deliberate anonymising gesture — he is shaped by the plot’s requirements, not allowed to be fully realised. A performer playing the Boy must resist underplaying him: the brief scenes by the canal carry the weight of Jo’s entire subsequent pregnancy.

A lighting designer might use the canal scenes as the one moment when the flat’s interior logic is softened — a lighting wash of cool blue fading at the edges to evoke the outdoors and winter water, with the performers lit from a lower angle to suggest evening rather than the flat’s harsh practical lights. This visual warmth-within-cold mirrors the emotional quality of the relationship: the most genuine warmth in the play exists in the coldest season.
exam_tip_html: For 8-mark performer questions, the most common mistake is writing “I would say this line angrily” without specifying what “angry” means in physical and vocal terms. You need to name the vocal quality (raised pitch and increased pace, with a hard consonant emphasis on the final word), the physical action (a step back, a turned shoulder, a dropped gaze) and anchor both to the named moment in the play. For 20-mark staging responses on character, you must address both performer and designer choices: a performer’s proxemics do not exist separately from the lighting state that exposes or conceals that proximity to the audience. Think of staging as a whole picture, not a checklist of separate skills.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jo operates on two registers — defensive wit and suppressed vulnerability — and a performer must make both visible through specific vocal and physical choices, not just state what Jo is feeling.
  • Helen should be played sympathetically as a woman shaped by limited options; Geof must be understood in the context of 1958 illegality, which makes his care for Jo a courageous act. Both characters require historical context to be performed at a high level.
  • The Boy’s brief presence carries disproportionate weight — the staging of his scenes with Jo (proxemics, lighting wash, warmth within cold) must communicate the genuine tenderness that makes the rest of the play's loss meaningful.

practice_questions.text: Identify one character in A Taste of Honey who is described as a queer art student.
What is meant by the term 'proxemics' in a theatrical context?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that proxemics refers to distance or spatial relationships between performers on stage; 1 mark for explaining that it is used to communicate meaning such as power, intimacy, hostility or vulnerability between characters.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director might use proxemics to communicate the change in Jo's relationship with the Boy across their scenes together.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of proxemics as a tool for communicating emotional distance or closeness (1), explanation of how starting with greater distance between Jo and the Boy signals her initial guardedness (1), explanation of how gradually reducing that distance communicates growing trust or affection (1), link to the effect this creates for the audience watching the relationship develop (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Jo, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate her two contrasting registers — defensive wit and suppressed vulnerability — in the scene when she is left alone after Helen departs with Peter.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both vocal and physical choices are named and specific, anchored to the moment after Helen's departure; vocal choices distinguish between the two registers (e.g. fast pace and sharp consonants for the wit; a drop in volume and a pause before a single syllable for the vulnerability); physical choices are equally specific (e.g. a sharp movement away from the door followed by stillness; a hand reaching towards where Helen stood then pulling back); the effect on the audience is clearly stated.

Secure: Both registers addressed; at least one specific vocal and one specific physical choice named for each; effect on audience identified; generally anchored to the named moment.

Developing: One register addressed more than the other; choices are relevant but generic ('sad voice', 'looks upset'); limited anchoring to the specific moment.

Emerging: Describes what Jo feels rather than how a performer would show it; no distinction between vocal and physical; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer might use lighting and costume to communicate the contrast between Helen and Jo to the audience throughout the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific lighting contrast between the two characters (1), explanation of how that lighting choice communicates something about each character's function or situation (1), identification of a costume choice that contrasts the two women (1), explanation of how that costume choice communicates their different relationships to femininity, class or age (1).

practice_questions.text: As a director staging A Taste of Honey, explain how you would use proxemics, blocking and design choices to communicate the contrasting relationships Jo has with Helen and with Geof. Refer to specific moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive, specific staging that addresses proxemics, blocking and at least two design disciplines (lighting, costume, set or sound) for both relationships; choices are anchored to named moments (e.g. Helen's return in Act Two, Geof and Jo making a home); each choice is justified with a clear effect on the audience; shows understanding of the thematic significance of the contrast between the two relationships; all choices are concrete rather than generic.

Secure: Both relationships addressed with at least one named moment each; proxemics and at least one design discipline covered; generally concrete choices; effect on audience identified.

Developing: Some staging ideas but mainly general; one relationship addressed more fully than the other; limited named moments; effect on audience implied not stated.

Emerging: Basic description of the two relationships without staging specificity; few or no named moments; descriptive rather than analytical.

Why does Geof's queer identity carry particular historical significance in A Taste of Honey?
options: It was seen as fashionable in Salford at the time
Homosexuality was illegal in Britain in 1958
Theatre Workshop had banned queer characters from its productions
Geof is the only working-class character in the play

The term used to describe the distance and spatial relationship between performers on stage is _____.
Match each character to their description:
right: A sharp-tongued 17-year-old with literary ambitions and suppressed vulnerability
Jo's restless, semi-alcoholic mother who leaves for Peter
A queer art student who moves in to care for Jo during her pregnancy

flashcard_questions.a: The distance and spatial relationship between performers, used to communicate meaning.

flashcard_questions.a: Homosexuality was illegal in Britain in 1958, making his choice to live with Jo courageous.

flashcard_questions.q: What word best describes Helen as a mother in A Taste of Honey?
What is a lighting special in theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: A focused beam of light on a specific performer or area, isolating them from the general wash.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a director use tableau?
flashcard_questions.a: A frozen stage picture at a dramatic moment to communicate meaning spatially.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Boy's occupation in A Taste of Honey?
flashcard_questions.a: He is a Black sailor on shore leave.
Coloured light covering the whole stage or large areas, creating a general ambient quality.

flashcard_questions.q: How old is Jo when the play begins?
What does Peter do that changes the structure of Act One?
flashcard_questions.a: He takes Helen away from Jo, leaving Jo alone.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Geof do for Jo in Act Two?
flashcard_questions.a: He moves in to care for her during her pregnancy, creating a makeshift family.

glossary_terms.definition: The distance and spatial relationship between performers on stage, used to communicate power, intimacy, hostility or vulnerability.
The area of the stage closest to the audience and directly in the middle, the most prominent position on a proscenium stage.
The planned arrangement of the whole stage picture at a specific dramatic moment, creating a frozen image that communicates meaning to the audience.
A focused beam of light directed at a specific performer or area of the stage, isolating them from the general wash.
A coloured light that covers the whole stage or large areas of it, creating a general ambient quality rather than focusing on a single performer.
When a performer speaks directly to the audience, stepping outside the scene to create an intimate or conspiratorial relationship with the house.
